# polars-online

> Streaming / online regression, clustering and regime models for Polars. A Rust core,
> reachable three ways with identical numerics: a chunk-fed `ModelBank` (its `fit`
> chunks a `LazyFrame`), a `LazyFrame` query that streams, and the `polars-online`
> command line over files. Memory grows with the models' state and the rows a delay or
> window holds, never with the rows passed, so a model fits a stream larger than RAM.

Python 3.12+, `polars>=1.37.0,<3`. `pip install polars-online`. `numpy` is an optional
extra, needed only by `ModelBank.gram()`, by `po.gram`, `po.corr`, `po.sim` and
`po.gbdt`, and by `bank.check()`'s collinearity and leakage checks, which report
`not_checked` without it. No pandas.

The two Python surfaces, in full:

```python
import polars as pl
import polars_online as po

spec = po.spec.ewridge(
    "ridge",
    targets=["ret"], features=["signal_a", "signal_b"],
    clock="ts",                    # a Datetime column, so the clock parameters are durations
    half_life=pl.duration(minutes=10), gap_cap=pl.duration(minutes=5),
    group="stock_id",              # one independent state per stock
)

# As a loop: feed chunks of any size; the state is yours to save
bank = po.ModelBank([spec])
for chunk in chunks:
    out = bank.fit_predict(chunk)     # a column of records per spec
bank.save("bank.state")

# As a query: the same numbers, streamed by polars, state written when the stream ends
(pl.scan_parquet("ticks/*.parquet")
   .online.fit_predict([spec], save_state="bank.state")
   .sink_parquet("fitted.parquet"))
```

**Rules that are easy to get wrong.**

- **A model is spelled the same way in both places**: the Python builder
  `po.spec.ewridge(...)` is `type = "ewridge"` in a spec dict or a TOML file, and so
  for every model. The old spelling, `ew_ridge`, is refused, naming `ewridge`.
- **Predictions are out-of-sample by construction.** A row's `pred` is computed from the
  state as it stands *before* the model learns that row's target. Never fit a row
  and then predict it: the `pred` the library returns is already out-of-sample.
- **Chunk invariance is a guarantee.** The same stream fed as one chunk or a thousand
  gives identical output, bit for bit, and a test enforces it. Only which rows carry
  `coef` (and `support_coef` and `se_coef` beside it) can move, by default: they sit on
  each group's last row not skipped in every chunk, so they follow the chunking. Under a cadence those rows do not move either: `coef_every` is a clock
  parameter, as `solve_every` is (`0` every row, `"5m"` a row once five minutes of the
  clock have passed), and `max_rows_between_coefs` writes one after that many rows.
- **Decay runs on the clock, not on row count.** A `Datetime`, `Date` or `Duration`
  clock takes its clock parameters (`half_life`, `gap_cap`, `window_size`, ...) as
  durations: `pl.duration(minutes=10)`, a `timedelta` or `"10m"`. A numeric clock takes
  plain numbers in its own units. Either mixture is refused, naming the parameter.
  `gap_cap`, `session` / `session_gap` and `restart_after_step_back` say what happens
  across a gap, a session boundary or a clock that steps back. A step back is
  refused unless `restart_after_step_back` is set and the step is larger, which resets
  the model. One no larger is a late row, refused.
- **A `clock` needs a `gap_cap`.** A spec that names a clock and no cap is refused:
  "gap_cap is required when clock is given". The cap is the most one step between two
  rows can age the state, in the clock's units, so a gap such as a weekend does not
  forget everything at once.
- **The clock need not be a time.** Sort by a feature, clock on it with a `gap_cap` in
  its units, and the half-life is a bandwidth in that feature's units. The fit is then
  a local regression in it (LOESS with a one-sided exponential kernel), and `ew_cov`
  clocked the same way gives local moments.
- **`weight_sum` is accumulated weight**, before the model learns this row and before its own decay —
  the same definition in every model. `min_weight` is in those units, so it is a
  weight, not a number of rows.
- **A zero-weight row is legal** and means "advance the clock, learn nothing", including
  as the first row of a stream.
- **Make a target from its row's columns as a column** before the bank,
  `lf.with_columns(ret=(pl.col("p") / pl.col("mid")).log())`, and name it in
  `targets`: a log ratio sits about zero, where `hit_rate` takes its sign. `po.target`
  only names a target's output fields.
- **Every spec adds one column**, named after the spec, each row a record of
  named fields. `weight_sum` is in every one.
  The linear models add `pred_<target>`, `resid_<target>` and `coef`, and diagnostics
  add theirs when switched on.
  [OUTPUTS.md](https://github.com/hgilde/polars-online/blob/main/docs/OUTPUTS.md) lists
  every model's fields, and `frame.online.unnest(specs)` flattens the column into plain
  columns.

**Every surface streams.** There is no in-memory-only form, and no expression
namespace: Polars hands a stateful user expression its whole column, so it cannot stream. The three surfaces, and how each loads and saves a state:

| surface | run it | load a state | save a state |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ModelBank`, fed chunks or handed a `LazyFrame` | `bank.fit_predict(chunk)` | `po.ModelBank.load(path)` | `bank.save(path)` |
| a query | `lf.online.fit_predict(...)` | `load_state=` | `save_state=` |
| the `polars-online` command line | `polars-online --config bank.toml` | `--load-state`, or `load_state` in the TOML | `--save-state`, or `save_state` in the TOML |

A state file is versioned msgpack, written atomically, and loads on macOS, Linux and
Windows alike.

## Start here

- [README](https://github.com/hgilde/polars-online#readme): the landing page -- what the
  library is, install, [a first fit](https://github.com/hgilde/polars-online#a-first-fit),
  the [example data](https://github.com/hgilde/polars-online#example-data)
  every other example reads, and [a map](https://github.com/hgilde/polars-online#where-to-go-next)
  from each task to its pages
- [Every feature](https://github.com/hgilde/polars-online/blob/main/docs/FEATURES.md): each model, function, method, shared
  parameter, flag and environment variable, a line each, linked
- [Five tasks](https://github.com/hgilde/polars-online/blob/main/docs/HIGHLIGHTS.md): model
  selection, a deployed signal, trees, monitoring, ticks
- [What every spec takes](https://github.com/hgilde/polars-online/blob/main/docs/MODELS.md#what-every-spec-takes): the parameters every
  model shares -- columns, clock and units, the clock's policy, a hard window, the warm-up
  gates -- and what the bank refuses
- [Models](https://github.com/hgilde/polars-online/blob/main/docs/MODELS.md): all 22, each with its recursion, its builder and its Rust
  source. [Choose a model](https://github.com/hgilde/polars-online/blob/main/docs/how-to/choose-a-model.md) says which for what
- [Every document](https://github.com/hgilde/polars-online/blob/main/docs/README.md): every guide, grouped by kind and task

## API reference

- [Spec builders](https://hgilde.github.io/polars-online/spec.html): every keyword
  and its default
- [ModelBank, fit_predict, predict](https://hgilde.github.io/polars-online/polars_online.html):
  the objects and functions the package exports
- [Frame namespaces](https://hgilde.github.io/polars-online/namespaces.html):
  `lf.online.*`, `df.online.*`
- [Evaluation](https://hgilde.github.io/polars-online/eval.html)
- [Gram accessors](https://hgilde.github.io/polars-online/gram.html)
- [Correlation toolkit](https://hgilde.github.io/polars-online/corr.html)
- [Stream transforms](https://hgilde.github.io/polars-online/stream.html)
- [Window operators](https://hgilde.github.io/polars-online/ops.html): `po.ewm_mean`,
  `po.ewm_sum`, `po.ewm_rate`, `po.ewm_quantile` (each looking ahead under `reverse=True`),
  `po.ewm_var`, `po.ewm_std` -- Polars expressions over a stream's clock -- and
  `po.increment`, a column's step from its last value, all run by
  `lf.online.with_windows(*exprs, **named, clock=...)` in one pass. A look-ahead one
  is also a spec's target, learned once its window has passed: `fit_predict`
  refuses an `embargo` shorter than its `window_size`
- [Training inputs for XGBoost and LightGBM](https://hgilde.github.io/polars-online/gbdt.html):
  `po.gbdt.xgboost_matrix`, `po.gbdt.lightgbm_dataset`, binned from Arrow IPC, Parquet
  or a query one chunk at a time, for data larger than memory (unstable)
- [Simulation](https://hgilde.github.io/polars-online/sim.html)
